name: Bones of the foot
func: Twenty-six bones that form the foot's arches. Together they carry your full body weight, absorb shock with every step, and turn the foot into a stiff lever for pushing off.

levels.kid:
Each of your feet has **26 bones**! That is a lot of bones for something so small.

There are big chunky bones at the back, like your **heel bone**. In the middle are long thin bones you can feel on the top of your foot. And at the front are tiny bones inside your **toes**.

The bones are shaped into a curve called an **arch**, like a little bridge. The arch acts like a spring, so when you walk, run or jump, your foot squishes a tiny bit and bounces back. That keeps your legs and back from getting jolted.
levels.hs:
The foot has **26 bones** in three groups.

The **tarsals** (7 bones) form the back and middle of the foot. The **talus** sits on top and connects to the tibia and fibula at the ankle; it has no muscles attached to it. Under it is the **calcaneus** (heel bone), the largest foot bone, where the Achilles tendon attaches. In front are the **navicular** on the inner side, the **cuboid** on the outer side, and three **cuneiforms** (medial, intermediate, lateral).

The **metatarsals** (5 bones) are the long bones of the forefoot, numbered 1 (big toe side) to 5. Their heads form the **ball of the foot**.

The **phalanges** (14 bones) are the toe bones: two in the big toe (**hallux**) and three in each other toe.

The bones are arranged into three **arches**: the **medial longitudinal arch** (the high inner arch), the **lateral longitudinal arch** (lower, on the outside) and the **transverse arch** across the midfoot. Ligaments, the **plantar fascia** and muscles hold the arches up. When you stand, weight passes from the tibia into the talus and spreads back to the heel and forward to the metatarsal heads.
levels.college:
**Regions:** the **hindfoot** (talus and calcaneus), **midfoot** (navicular, cuboid, cuneiforms) and **forefoot** (metatarsals and phalanges).

**Key joints:** the **talocrural (ankle) joint** allows dorsiflexion and plantarflexion. The **subtalar joint** between talus and calcaneus is the main site of **inversion and eversion**. The **transverse tarsal (Chopart) joint** combines the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints. The **tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) joint** links the midfoot to the forefoot; the base of the second metatarsal is recessed between the cuneiforms like a keystone, and the strong **Lisfranc ligament** runs from the medial cuneiform to it.

**Notable landmarks:** the **sustentaculum tali** is a shelf on the medial calcaneus supporting the talus, with the flexor hallucis longus tendon running beneath it. The **tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal** receives fibularis brevis. Two **sesamoid bones** under the first metatarsal head sit in the flexor hallucis brevis tendons.

**Arch support:** the medial arch is supported by the **spring (plantar calcaneonavicular) ligament**, which cradles the head of the talus, by the plantar fascia, and dynamically by tibialis posterior and flexor hallucis longus. Fibularis longus and tibialis anterior form a "stirrup" under the midfoot.

**Windlass mechanism:** extending the toes at push-off winds the plantar fascia around the metatarsal heads, raising the arch and turning the foot into a rigid lever.

**Relations:** the posterior tibial artery and tibial nerve pass behind the medial malleolus through the **tarsal tunnel**, dividing into medial and lateral plantar branches in the sole; the dorsalis pedis artery is felt over the dorsum, lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.
levels.phd:
The foot is a hybrid of a flexible adaptor and a rigid lever, and this switch is driven by subtalar and midtarsal mechanics. When the subtalar joint **everts (pronates)**, the axes of the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints become more parallel, unlocking the midfoot so it can conform to uneven ground. When it **inverts (supinates)**, the axes diverge, locking the midfoot for propulsion. This "midtarsal locking" model is classic, although modern multi-segment motion analysis shows the midfoot is more mobile than the textbook suggested.

The **talus** is about 60% covered by articular cartilage and receives blood mainly through vessels entering the neck and sinus tarsi, especially the **artery of the tarsal canal** (from the posterior tibial artery) and the artery of the sinus tarsi. Its body is supplied in a largely retrograde way, from the neck backwards, so neck fractures can cut off supply and cause **avascular necrosis**.

The human foot is a recent evolutionary specialisation. Compared with apes, humans have a robust calcaneal tuber, an adducted non-grasping hallux, a rigid midfoot and a permanent longitudinal arch. Footprints at **Laetoli** (about 3.66 million years ago) show a humanlike gait, though researchers still debate how arched those early feet were.

Energy storage is substantial: the arch and plantar fascia act as springs that return a meaningful fraction of mechanical energy during running, together with the Achilles tendon. **Intrinsic foot muscles** act as an active "foot core", modulating arch stiffness, a concept supported by nerve block experiments that reduce arch control.
levels.expert:
**Exam:** inspect the arches while standing (pes planus or cavus), the heel from behind (valgus), and look for the **too-many-toes sign** (more lateral toes visible from behind in a flattened, abducted foot). The **single-leg heel raise** tests tibialis posterior; failure suggests **posterior tibial tendon dysfunction**, the commonest cause of adult acquired flatfoot. Apply the **Ottawa foot rules** for trauma: X-ray if there is tenderness at the navicular or base of the fifth metatarsal, or inability to bear weight.

**Fifth metatarsal fractures:** an avulsion of the tuberosity usually heals well; a **Jones fracture** at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction is in a watershed area and prone to nonunion, often needing longer protection or screw fixation.

**Lisfranc injuries** are easily missed. Look for plantar bruising and a **fleck sign** (avulsion fragment) between the first and second metatarsal bases; weight-bearing X-rays or CT help. Missed injuries cause chronic arthritis.

**Calcaneus fractures** follow falls from height; **Böhler's angle** is reduced on lateral X-ray, and associated spine fractures must be checked. **Talar neck fractures** are graded by **Hawkins**; a later subchondral lucency (**Hawkins sign**) suggests revascularisation, a good sign.

Other conditions: **stress fractures** of the second metatarsal (march fracture), **tarsal coalition** in adolescents causing rigid flatfoot, **hallux valgus** (bunion), **Charcot neuroarthropathy** in people with diabetic neuropathy, and **Morton's neuroma** between metatarsal heads. **Tarsal tunnel syndrome** compresses the tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus.

keyPoints: Talus links the leg to the foot; calcaneus is the heel
Three arches; windlass mechanism stiffens the foot at push-off
Jones fracture and Lisfranc injuries are classic misses

test.q: How many bones are in one foot?
Which tarsal bone forms the heel?
test.explain: The calcaneus is the largest foot bone and receives the Achilles tendon.

test.q: Which joint is the main site of inversion and eversion?
test.explain: Inversion/eversion occur mostly between the talus and calcaneus.

test.q: Why is a talar neck fracture worrying?
choices: It always damages the Achilles tendon
It blocks the dorsalis pedis artery
Blood supply to the talar body can be cut off
test.explain: The body's supply runs back from the neck, so neck fractures risk avascular necrosis.

test.q: A fracture at the base of the fifth metatarsal in a watershed zone is a ______ fracture.
test.explain: It is prone to nonunion, unlike a simple tuberosity avulsion.
